title: About
text:
Understanding and predicting the behavioural drivers of epidemic dynamics — and evaluating whether the interventions we build on them are worth the money.

I’m Luke Burton, a PhD Researcher in the Department of Infectious Disease Epidemiology and Dynamics, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine.
My doctoral work asks how social contact, mobility and attitude data can be used to understand and forecast the behavioural drivers of epidemic dynamics — the messy, human half of why outbreaks unfold the way they do. It builds on a background in mathematics and health data science, and on earlier work using branching process models to estimate the probability that an introduction becomes a major epidemic.
Alongside that I work in health economics, on cost-utility modelling and economic evaluation of blood-borne virus screening interventions: coding hepatitis B progression models, evaluating TB IGRA testing in high-risk groups, and micro-costing digitally enhanced BBV testing.

title: Research
text:
Projects

Behavioural drivers of epidemic dynamics
The doctoral project. Social contact, mobility and attitude data carry signal about how people actually behave during an outbreak — who mixes with whom, how that changes under pressure, and how quickly it reverts. The question is whether that signal can be used not just to explain epidemic dynamics after the fact, but to forecast them.


Economic evaluation of blood-borne virus screening
NIHR-funded work on whether blood-borne virus testing interventions are worth what they cost: coding hepatitis B progression models to evaluate emergency department opt-out testing, assessing TB IGRA testing in high-risk groups, and micro-costing digitally enhanced BBV testing.


Vaccine responses and vaccine equity
Earlier work using machine learning to understand vaccine responses to influenza, and modelling vaccine equity and trachoma resurgence.
